The proposed answer of 38 is incorrect, because the solution misses most of the valid values of n.

**Derivation.** Suppose B and C are friends. Any enemy A of B must also be an enemy of C, because the friend of an enemy is an enemy. So friends have the same set of enemies, and the sets are equal since each guest has exactly 12 enemies.

Friendship is therefore transitive. Suppose B~C and C~D are friends but B and D are enemies. Then D is in B's enemy set, which equals C's enemy set, so C and D would be enemies, a contradiction.

So the guests split into friendship classes, where everyone within a class is friends and everyone in different classes is enemies. Each guest's enemies are everyone outside their class, so n − s = 12, where s is the class size. All classes have the same size s, so n = ks for some number of classes k. Then ks = s + 12, which gives s(k − 1) = 12.

The possible class sizes are the divisors of 12: s = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The corresponding values of n = s + 12 are 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 24. Each works, since a complete multipartite graph with equal parts has the required properties.

The sum is 13 + 14 + 15 + 16 + 18 + 24 = 100.

The proposed solution found only n = 13 and n = 25. The value 25 is invalid: a (25, 12, 0, 11) strongly regular graph would have no friends-of-enemies structure of this kind, and it does not satisfy the transitivity condition. Its reasoning was also not rigorous.

VERDICT: REJECT
